Struggling San Francisco solar startup Aurora Solar has shed more staff and named a new CEO.

Company representatives confirmed the cuts but declined to say how many people Aurora let go. In an email, company co-founder and outgoing CEO Chris Hopper blamed the layoffs on the One Big Beautiful Bill Act that Congress passed and President Donald Trump signed this past summer.

That law ends federal tax credits for new residential solar-panel and home-battery systems at the end of this year and phases out such incentives for commercial solar projects. Aurora offers software that helps installers design and sell solar systems.

The “One Big Beautiful Bill was not favorable to our industry,” Hopper said in the email. “We remain optimistic about the future of solar, but did have to make a reduction in force that was necessary to align the business with the post-OBBB landscape.”

Hopper said he is stepping down as CEO to become Aurora’s executive chairman. Charlie Herche, formerly the company’s senior vice president of finance, is replacing Hopper as chief executive, according to a company representative.

Although happening around the same time as the cuts, the management change was “unrelated,” Hopper said.

“I'm still very much involved as Executive Chairman, just handing off my day-to-day responsibilities as CEO to focus my time on other areas of the business,” he said.

Hopper and other Aurora representatives declined to say when the company laid off staff or what percentage of its workforce was affected by the cuts, which represented at least Aurora’s third round of layoffs since January 2024.

As of Friday morning, state employment officials said they had not received a mass-layoff notice from the company. Such notices — which the state requires when a company with at least 75 employees lets go of 50 or more of them within a 30-day period — include the number of people being laid off and the dates of the cuts.

At least 10 Aurora employees have indicated publicly on LinkedIn they are looking for new jobs. At least two of them indicated in posts on the site they lost their positions at the company this week.

“Hi everyone! I’m seeking a new role and would appreciate your support,” Luis Munoz — a senior professional service engineer who had been with Aurora since August 2023, according to his LinkedIn page — said in a post Monday.

Munoz did not respond to a request for comment about the layoffs.

According to notices it filed with the state, Aurora [laid off 115 people](https://www.sfexaminer.com/news/technology/sf-layoffs-continue-with-salesforce-cisco-cutting-jobs/article_b31b33a4-d69c-11ee-a4b0-2f47bbf0c97d.html) based at its San Francisco office in January 2024 and [another 58 this past January](https://www.sfexaminer.com/news/technology/sf-green-tech-startup-aurora-solar-laying-off-dozens-again/article_a5fc0dbc-d450-11ef-95d2-03eab04fe214.html). But posts by former employees on LinkedIn and a spreadsheet compiled by them indicated those latter cuts [actually affected dozens more people](https://www.sfexaminer.com/news/technology/aurora-solar-layoffs-likely-wider-than-previously-reported/article_45cdb7b6-de72-11ef-90b8-8bcde7f718ef.html).

Boosted by rapid adoption of solar systems, particularly in California, Aurora saw its fortunes and valuation soar in the late 2010s and earlier this decade. Between 2019 and early 2022, it raised $524 million in venture funding and saw its valuation jump from $63 million to $4 billion, according to data from PitchBook, a venture-industry research firm.

But the company has been hit in recent years by a [sharp downturn in solar installations](https://www.thenewlede.org/2025/09/rooftop-solar-california-utilities-clean-energy/), particularly in its home state. In 2022, the California Public Utilities Commission [cut by 75% the amount utilities pay for the power residential customers send](http://www.sfexaminer.com/news/politics/ca-votes-to-slash-rooftop-solar-credits/article_c9bb65ce-7cd0-11ed-8250-2bf61d4b41d9.html) from their solar arrays to the electrical grid. That move increased the time it would take to pay off such systems, decreasing one of the incentive for installing them.

The solar-subsidy cuts under Trump’s tax-and-spending law have only added to the company and the industry’s woes, Hopper said.

“The industry was set to recover, but unfortunately this bill means US residential solar is looking at another year of decline before it's set to grow again,” he said in the email.
